title: Who May Say the Review Is Finished?
thesis: Someone who knowingly supplies an operative organizational authorization must exercise reasonable care concerning a serious objection left untreated by its supporting review, qualifying or withholding that authorization where reasonably needed despite a narrower specialist remit.
contribution: A bounded specification of care for local and nondecisive operative authorizations, distinguishing moral requirements from institutional clearance and explaining why a transfer of unfinished assessment must remain connected to implementation.
strongest_objection: The account may specify familiar reasonable-care and assistance duties without enough independent explanatory novelty; the normative bridge from operative authorization to the required response needs broader philosophical testing.
originality_limitations: Bounded excerpt reading and keyword search only. Broad many-hands, role morality and answerability ideas are established; Kahl also discusses procedural authority and decisions about outstanding risk. No priority claim across professional handoffs, assurances, institutional powers, organizational voice or negligence is established.
open_questions: Which institutional practices count as supplying operative authorization rather than information?
When does reasonable deference to a superior defeat the employee’s apparent concern?
How should serious-objection thresholds and proportional costs be specified?
How far do duties concerning redundant operative permissions extend beyond the controlled case?
Does the specification make a sufficiently original philosophical contribution?
